content: Freckles are small, pigmented spots that appear on the exposed skin or mucous membranes of individuals with fair complexions, making them more visible. The presence of freckles is primarily determined by genetics and is associated with a variant of the melanocortin-1 receptor (MC1R) gene, which is a dominant trait. Freckles can also be induced by prolonged exposure to sunlight, such as during tanning. When ultraviolet (UV) rays from the sun penetrate the skin, they activate melanocytes, which can lead to freckles becoming darker and more numerous, although the distribution of melanin remains uneven. Freckles are often linked to individuals with fair or pale skin, and they are commonly associated with light-colored hair, such as blonde or red hair, with red hair being more strongly correlated. Freckles predominantly appear on the face but can also develop on any area of the skin exposed to sunlight. They are rare in infants but become more common in children before puberty. However, freckles tend to be less prevalent in adults. In children, temporary freckles may develop due to insufficient melanin production to protect their skin from harmful UV rays. These freckles often fade after puberty as melanin production increases. Individuals with the fairest skin may continue to have freckles into adulthood, indicating a genetic predisposition for freckling. Freckles that have been altered or lightened using creams or laser treatments will reappear upon sun exposure if the skin is not adequately protected. However, freckles may fade with age in some cases. It is important to note that freckles are not a skin disorder. Nevertheless, individuals with a genetic predisposition to freckles may be more susceptible to sunburn and skin cancer. Therefore, they should take extra precautions to protect their skin by using a daily sunscreen with a minimum SPF of 15. Historically, during the Middle Ages and up until the early 15th century in Europe, an abundance of freckles, often referred to as witch marks or witch spots, was associated with witchcraft. This belief was likely due to the genetic pairing of freckles with red hair, which was also considered a characteristic of witches. There are two main types of freckles. The first type, known as ephelides, is a genetic trait. Ephelides are flat, light brown or reddish freckles that tend to fade during the winter months. They are more common in individuals with light complexions and can be suppressed with regular use of sunscreen. The second type, commonly referred to as liver spots or sun spots, does not fade in the winter. These freckles develop after years of cumulative sun exposure and are more frequently observed in older individuals. This type of freckle is also known as lentigines.
